transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my family brought me in. See, we were down at the county fair, and I was giving my talk. But then I just climbed right up onto the tractor. I kept jerking the controls all around to show the crowd the new pattern. I had to show them the pattern. I couldn't make myself stop, either, even with everybody yelling at me to get down. 

Yelling so loud... kind of like the auctioneer over at the livestock pavilion. Have you ever been to the livestock pavilion when they're selling the Duroc hogs? My daddy used to raise Durocs back in the 70s. Finest pork you'll ever eat, but they are stubborn creatures. You gotta mix their feed just right, mostly corn, but you add a little molasses to it to sweeten it up. We had this one sow, broke out of her pen and ate half a field of sweet corn before my brother found her sleeping under the combine... I always told him to check the latch on that gate, but he never listened.
Have you ever had periods before this—lasting days or weeks—where you felt extremely high, energetic, or irritable, or on the other hand, very depressed and low, different from how you feel now?

Well, high and irritable, sure... I get like that. Some mornings I wake up and I just feel like the whole valley is opening up right there for me. I'll be standing out on the porch just grinning at absolutely nothing, feeling like I could run the whole county. But then, if one of the hired hands questions how I'm doing things, or if my wife comes out and tells me I need to slow down, I just snap. I snap at 'em like they've insulted the family name! 

And you know, speaking of the family name, my grandfather was the one who originally settled that part of the valley. Came out here with nothing but two mules and a buckboard wagon. Named those mules Pete and Repete. Always thought that was a hoot. Repete, though, he had this terrible habit of chewing on the wooden fence posts. We had to paint the wood with creosote just to get him to stop ruining the boundary lines. Creosote smells just awful, especially when the July heat bakes it. Smells a lot like the tar we used on the roof of the old barn before the big storm of '93... we were up there for three days straight just slathering it on before the rain came. My shoulders ached for a month after that.
Have you ever, at another time in your life, gone through a period lasting two weeks or more where you felt very sad, low, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

Sad? No, I wouldn't say I've been sad for weeks on end. I don't have time for that kind of moping around, not with the farm to run. I mean, sure, sometimes you get a bad season and it gets you down for a minute, but you just keep moving. 

Speaking of bad seasons, back in '08, we had a drought that nearly wiped out the whole alfalfa crop. I remember walking out into the field, and the dirt was just cracking under my boots like peanut brittle. Peanut brittle... my grandmother used to make the best peanut brittle every Christmas. She’d spread it out on this big marble slab she got from an old bank in town that was being torn down. The bank had these massive brass doors, too. I always wondered what happened to those doors. Probably melted down for scrap. Shame, really. They don't make things like they used to. Nowadays, everything is just cheap aluminum that bends if you look at it wrong. We put up a new aluminum shed last year, and a good gust of wind came through and buckled the whole north wall. Had to spend three days bracing it with two-by-fours...
How long has this current stretch of feeling really high, energetic, or irritable—like what happened at the fair—been going on? Has it been going on for a week or more without letting up?

Well, a week? Try months. If I look back at the past year or so, I'd say I've spent about ten months of it just... charged up like a live wire. No sleep, just nonstop, going and going. 

Going... like that old Ford tractor we used to have. The blue one, you know? My dad bought it second-hand from a guy over in Shelbyville. Shelbyville's got that big water tower painted like a peach. Never understood why they painted it like a peach when they don't even grow peaches over there. It's mostly soybeans. Soybeans are a good rotation crop, though. Puts the nitrogen right back in the soil. You gotta respect the soil. If you don't take care of the dirt, the dirt won't take care of you. That's what my uncle always said. He was a smart man, my uncle. He could witch for water with a willow branch. I saw him do it once behind the old smokehouse. The branch just dipped right down, nearly pulled out of his hands. We dug down about twelve feet right there and hit the sweetest spring water you ever tasted. Cold, too. Cold enough to crack your teeth if you drank it too fast...

During these months of feeling revved up, have you experienced anything like hearing voices or seeing things that others couldn't, or having beliefs—like having special powers or a special mission—that others told you weren't true?

Well, yeah, during all those months when I was hardly sleeping at all, just pushing that farm expansion day and night... I started hearing them. Voices, I mean. They were coming right out of the irrigation lines. Just whispering at me while the water was running. And I'd look at the yield maps we had printed out, and I could read these warnings in them, clear as day, telling me what was coming. 

Coming... like that storm back in '98. The one that took down the old oak tree by the driveway. That tree must have been a hundred years old. My grandfather used to tie his horses to it. Horses are funny creatures, you know. They get spooked by the strangest things. Had a mare once, beautiful chestnut thing, who would absolutely refuse to walk past a white bucket. Blue bucket? Fine. Red bucket? No problem. But a white bucket? She'd rear up and act like it was a rattlesnake. Rattlesnakes used to be real bad up on the ridge. We'd have to take a shotgun up there just to check the fence lines. I always preferred a 12-gauge for that. Gives a good spread. My brother, though, he always swore by a .410. Said it was lighter to carry. He carried that .410 all over the county...
